title: Tyre and Sidon
lead: Tyre and Sidon were the chief cities of Phoenicia, on the coast of modern Lebanon, famous for sea trade, purple dye and cedar. They were Israel's trading partners under David and Solomon, the target of prophetic oracles, and places Jesus visited.

sections.h: Tyre and Sidon across the Bible
sections.b: Genesis names Sidon as Canaan's firstborn (Genesis 10:15), and Tyre appears as a fortified city on the border of Asher (Joshua 19:29). Hiram of Tyre sent David and Solomon cedar, craftsmen and sailors (2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Kings 5:1–12), but Ahab's marriage to Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians, brought Baal worship into Israel (1 Kings 16:31). The prophets announced the fall of these proud trading cities: Isaiah 23, Jeremiah 47:4, Ezekiel 26–28, Joel 3:4–8, Amos 1:9–10 and Zechariah 9:2–4. After the exile the people of Sidon and Tyre again supplied cedar for the temple (Ezra 3:7). Jesus healed the daughter of a woman from the region (Mark 7:24–30) and said that Tyre and Sidon would have repented if they had seen his works (Matthew 11:21–22). Paul found disciples in Tyre (Acts 21:3–6), and Revelation's lament over Babylon draws on the prophets' laments over Tyre (Revelation 18:9–19).

sections.b: Tyre stood partly on a rocky island off the coast and partly on the mainland facing it. Its colonies reached Cyprus, North Africa (Carthage), Sicily and Spain. Assyria besieged and taxed it; Nebuchadnezzar besieged it for thirteen years (Ezekiel 29:18); and in 332 BC Alexander the Great built a causeway to the island and took it. The causeway silted up into the isthmus on which the modern city stands.
